A social dialect is really called a “social REGISTER” of a specifc language. It refers to the type of speech,
pronunciaton, and vocabulary used to communicate in the language with a specifc social class or group
with in the greater society. A regional dialect, on the other hand, is one that is strictly defned by
geography, and as such, is used among all people of all social classes/groups within that geography. It’s
a natural deviaton from the standard dialect through a long process of language evoluton, rather than
a social constructon used to more efectvely communicate between those of diferent socio-economic
status within a given area sharing the same standard language.

﻿Eng506 Assignment No.1 2020-2021

Q1. Define the term language planning as given by Brutt-Griffler (2002). List two characteristics of ‘Top down’ and ‘Bottom up’ language policy each. Also, explain five factors which determine the place of a language in language policy (2+4+4+10= 20 Marks)
Solution:
Language Planning
“Deliberate efforts to influence the behavior of others with respect to the acquisition, structure, or functional allocation of their language codes”
Cooper cited in Brutt-Griffler, 2002
Top down language policy
•	Formulated by authorities (governments, commissions etc.) and imposed on speech communities
Top down language policy
•	Language policy is conceived as a unidirectional process
•	Instruments of social control
•	Tools for the achievement of ideological objectives
Theory of linguistic imperialism
Takes for granted that the colonizing nation possesses the power to impose its will on the subjugated population
Bottom up language policy
•	Speech communities as active contributors to the shaping of the language policy
•	Codetermine the context
•	Seize the initiative from the institutional planners
Bottom up language policy
•	Not a unilateral process
•	Policy is an outcome of interplay between conflicting aims
Language policy
The place of a language in language policy is determined by:
•	Population
•	Prestige
•	Status
•	Functionality
•	Nationalism
Language policy in inner circle countries
•	English is the language of the majority
•	The issues is the role to be given to minority languages
•	Status planning involves different dialects of English
Language policy in outer circle countries
•	Only a minority of population is proficient in English
•	Despite being a minority language, English is powerful
Language policy in outer circle countries
•	Used by the elite
•	Language policy revolves around the role of English
•	The functionality of English is recognized and accepted
Language policy in expanding-circle countries
•	English lacks a strong population base
•	No official status
•	Enjoys a great deal of prestige
•	Has instrumental value
Language policy in expanding-circle countries
•	Used and learned as a foreign language
•	Acceleration in use due to globalization
•	Features prominently in language policy discourse

Q. What is Englishization?

Englishization refers to the process where English becomes increasingly used in various domains,
often influencing local languages and cultures.

Q. Describe the status of Japanese English.

English in Japan lacks an internal reason for promotion. Japanese is the medium of instruction and
government business. There is a cline of proficiency, with a small segment fluent in English. There
is also significant nativization, with many English borrowings.

Q. What are three factors that contribute to language policy?

   ❖ Population,
   ❖ prestige, and
   ❖ functionality.

Q. Define "death of a minority language."

The disappearance of a language due to factors like cultural assimilation, demographic
submersion, and globalization.

Q. What is the role of English in Europe?

English is the biggest de facto lingua franca in Europe, widely used in formal education, business,
and the EU apparatus.

Q. Describe the status of English in Southeast Asia.

English is secure in Singapore, in demand in the Philippines, undergoing revival in Malaysia, and
remains the dominant foreign language in other Southeast Asian countries.

Q. What is the current status of English in the Philippines?

English is widely used in education and governance. There was a shift toward Filipino but a return
to English due to globalization.

Q. How is Chinese developing as an emerging global language?

Chinese is growing due to economic development, globalization, and policies like the Belt and
Road Initiative.

Q. What determines the place of a language in language policy?

   ❖ Population,
   ❖ prestige,

   ❖ status, and
   ❖ functionality.

Q. Explain the difference between top-down and bottom-up language policies.

Top-down policies are imposed by governments, while bottom-up policies arise from community
needs and practices.

Q. What are the multilingual features of inner, outer, and expanding circles?

   ❖ Inner: English as the native language;
   ❖ Outer: English coexists with local languages;
   ❖ Expanding: English as a foreign language.

Q. Name three components of the outer and expanding circle context.

   ❖ Use in education,
   ❖ government, and
   ❖ international communication.

Q. How can English be maintained as an international language?

   ❖ Through continued global usage,
   ❖ adaptation to local needs, and
   ❖ maintaining its role in education and commerce.

Q. What challenges arise when compiling a dictionary?

   ❖ Standardization,
   ❖ inclusion of new words, and
   ❖ balancing regional variations.

Q. What is the significance of corpus sources in language studies?

Corpus sources provide empirical data for linguistic analysis, helping to track language evolution.

Q. What is the orthodox view of SLA?

SLA is seen as a cognitive process involving stages of acquisition.

Q. Who are the participants of SLA research?

   ❖ Learners,
   ❖ teachers, and
   ❖ researchers.

Q. Define communicative competence.

The ability to use language effectively in different social contexts.

Q. What are the two purposes of competence analysis?

Understanding language proficiency and identifying learning gaps.

Q. What is the myth of the native speaker as the ideal teacher?

The belief that native speakers are inherently better teachers, ignoring pedagogical training.

Q. How do non-native speakers perceive World English?

As a tool for communication rather than as a single standard variety.

Q. What problems do learners face while learning English? Mention three.

   ❖ Pronunciation difficulties,
   ❖ lack of exposure, and
   ❖ grammatical complexities.

Q. What is testing in ELT?

Assessment of language proficiency using standardized tests.

Q. What are two characteristics of language in Japanese English?

Insertion of vowels in consonant clusters and semantic shifts in vocabulary.

Q. How is English taught and learned in Singapore?

Through a pro-English policy, serving as a unifying language.

Q. What are two factors that influence ELT practices?

Economic demands and government policies.

Q. Why do bilingual women choose to speak English? Mention two reasons.

   ❖ Economic opportunities and
   ❖ social mobility.

Q. How do women adopt the dominant language?

Through education and workplace interactions.

Q: Difference between Regional and Social dialect.
 A social dialect is really called a “social REGISTER” of a
specific language. It refers to the type of speech, pronunciation, and vocabulary
used to communicate in the language with a specific social class or group with in
the greater society. A regional dialect, on the other hand, is one that is strictly
defined by geography, and as such, is used among all people of all social
classes/groups within that geography. It’s a natural deviation from the standard
dialect through a long process of language evolution, rather than a social
construction used to more effectively communicate between those of different
socio-economic status within a given area sharing the same standard language.

language) for speakers of different native languages.

Q: semantics shifts of African language.
In this article the phenomenon of semantic change as it manifests itself in a variety
of loanwords or adoptives from different Bantu languages is investigated. After a
discussion of the notion ‘semantic change’ several factors which play a role in such
changes are considered, e.g. ellipsis, analogy, metonymy, metaphor, folk
etymology, etc. It is shown that meaning change may result in the generalization,
specialization or radical change in a word's meaning, as well as in changes in the
emotive content of words. As far as the latter is concerned, the important role
played by taboo and euphemism is focussed upon.

﻿ENG506 GDB 2023-Solution By Pin✌️.

The statement that Pakistani learners face a dual challenge of maintaining their cultural identity while learning the English language holds validity. Language acquisition is inherently tied to culture, and learners often encounter a delicate balance between adopting a new linguistic framework and preserving their cultural roots.

English, as a global lingua franca, is often associated with Western culture. Pakistani learners, while mastering the language, may encounter influences that could potentially dilute or overshadow their rich cultural heritage. This challenge arises as they navigate between the cultural nuances embedded in their native language and the linguistic expectations of English.

However, it's essential to recognize that language is a dynamic medium for cultural expression. Pakistani learners can embrace English while concurrently incorporating their cultural identity into the language. This integration not only enriches the English they learn but also reinforces the importance of cultural diversity.

Efforts to strike this balance involve incorporating elements of Pakistani literature, history, and traditions into English language education. By doing so, learners can find a harmonious coexistence between linguistic proficiency and cultural preservation. In this way, the dual challenge becomes an opportunity for a more inclusive and culturally aware approach to language learning.
eng506-glossary-by-asfand-yarr-pdf:
ENG506_Glossary

1. Acculturation :The process by which a human being acquires the culture of a
   particular society from infancy
2. Code Mixing :Code-mixing is the mixing of two or more languages or language
   varieties in speech. Some scholars use the terms "code-mixing" and "code-
   switching" interchangeably, especially in studies of syntax, morphology, and
   other formal aspects of language.
3. Code Switching :The practice of alternating between two or more languages or
   varieties of language in conversation
4. Colonialism :The policy or practice of acquiring full or partial political control
   over another country, occupying it with settlers, and exploiting it economically
5. Communicative Competence :Communicative competence is a term in
   linguistics which refers to a language user's grammatical knowledge of syntax,
   morphology, phonology and the like, as well as social knowledge about how and
   when to use utterances appropriately.
6. Complacence :A feeling of smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's
   achievements
7. Contact Literature :The literature written in distinctive varieties of English is
   called contact literature.
8. Corpus Analysis :Qualitative corpus analysis is a methodology for pursuing in-
   depth investigations of linguistic phenomena, as grounded in the context of
   authentic, communicative situations that are digitally stored as language corpora
   and made available for access, retrieval, and analysis via computer.
9. Creoles :A creole is a language that has developed from a mixture of different
   languages and has become the main language in a particular place.

By ASFAND YARR

                             ENG506_Glossary

10. Creolisation :Creolisation is the process in which Creole cultures emerge in
   the New World. As a result of colonization there was a mixture among people of
   Indigenous American, West African and European descent, which came to be
   understood as Creolisation.
11. Descriptivism :The doctrine that the meanings of ethical or aesthetic terms
   and statements are purely descriptive rather than prescriptive, evaluative, or
   emotive
12. Discourse :Discourse refers to a unit of language longer than a single
   sentence.
13. Foreign Language :A foreign language is a language originally from another
   country. It is also a language not spoken in the native country of the person
   referred to, i.e., an English speaker living in Spain can say that Spanish is a
   foreign language to him or her.
14. Globalisation :This is a process of interaction and integration among the
   people, companies, and governments of different nations.
15. Institutionalization :The official recognition and acceptance of a language is
   termed as institutionalization
16. Interlanguage :A language or form of language having features of two others,
   typically a pidgin or a version produced by a foreign learner
17. International Language :Sometimes called universal language, a language
   intended to be used by people of different linguistic background to facilitate
   communication among them and to reduce the misunderstandings and
   antagonisms caused by language differences. An international language is
   usually intended not to supplant existing mother tongue but to play a secondary
   or auxiliary role as it furthers international communication.

18. Lexical :Relating to the words or vocabulary of a language
19. Lexicon :A lexicon is the knowledge that a native speaker has about a
   language.
20. Lingua Franca :A language that is adopted as a common language between
   speakers whose native languages are different
21. Linguicism :Kangas defined linguicism as the "ideologies and structures
   which are used to legitimate, effectuate, and reproduce unequal division of power
   and resources (both material and non-material) between groups which are defined
   on the basis of language".
22. Linguistic Diversity :It is a way to talk about varied types of traits including
   language family, grammar, and vocabulary.
23. Linguistic Imperialism :Linguistic imperialism is the imposition of one
   language on speakers of other languages. It also knows as linguistic nationalism,
   linguistic dominance, and language imperialism.
24. Monogenesis :The hypothetical origination of language or of a surname from
   a single source at a particular place and time
25. Morphology :Morphology is the study of words, how they are formed, and
   their relationship to other words in the same language.
26. Multilingual :A person with an ability to speak more than two languages
27. Native Language :A first language, native language or mother/father tongue
   (also known as arterial language or L1) is a language that a person has been
   exposed to from birth or within the critical period.
28. Nativization :Nativization is the process whereby a language gains native
   speakers. This happens necessarily where a second language used by adult
   parents becomes the native language of their children.

By ASFAND YARR

29. Phonology :The system of contrastive relationships among the speech sounds
   that constitute the fundamental components of a language or the study of
   phonological relationships within a language or between different languages
30. Pidginisation :Pidginisation is a linguistic process that occurs when people
   who do not speak the same language come into contact. It involves the
   simplification of the contacting language and the exploitation of linguistic
   common denominators.
31. Pidgins :A grammatically simplified form of a language, typically English,
   Dutch, or Portuguese, some elements of which are taken from local languages,
   used for communication between people not sharing a common language
32. Polygenesis :The hypothetical origination of language or of a surname from
   a number of independent sources in different places at different times

                                     English as a Global Language

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course Learning Theories

        The course gives an engaging overview of the development and concept of World Englishes. The course
discusses the role of English as a single global language all over the world and its advantages for the world as
well as the dangers for the minor languages. The course also describes various political, social and historical
contexts which led to the spread of English throughout the world and eventually caused it to become a lingua
franca.

The course aims to:
    understand globalization, global language and the need of a global language
    comprehend the relation between language and identity and the dominance of a global language over
       minor languages.
    have a conceptual understanding of English as native, second, foreign and international language and the
       factors affecting them.
Topic-001: Globalization

         World Englishes is a term coined by BrajKachru (an Indian-American linguist) initially to refer to the
institutionalized varieties of English. Now the term refers to various varieties of English across the world. The
pluralization of World English in the title refers to the large number of varieties that English is accrued as a result
of its contact with sociolinguistic context. It means that English is no longer used by native English speakers in
native English speaking countries like America, Australia, New Zealand, etc. Now English is also used by non-
native English speakers in non-native English speaking countries for various professional, official and
educational purposes. These countries include Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, etc. These distinct
varieties are grouped together under the heading of World Englishes.

         Globalization refers to a great number of things taking place in the world and their interconnectedness. It
is a process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments of different nations. This
interaction can take various forms, e.g. political cooperation among countries with the hope that this kind of co-
operation will help prevent disputes or in case of a dispute will help resolve such disputes. Some examples are
SAARC, European Union and NATO. Another form that this interaction can take is through sharing of ideas and
information. In today’s world sharing of information takes place through social media and internet. This can also
take place with the help of TV programs, films and books.
         Trade and exchange of resources greatly enhances this interaction. Countries like America sell their
finished products and technologies to countries which lack them. Similarly, developing countries sell their
natural resources to the developed countries which need them.
Globalization is not a new phenomenon. For thousands of years countries and later corporation have been selling
and buying things from far off lands. Similarly, for centuries, countries have been investing in enterprises in
foreign countries. It increased as result of technological development. Globalization has also led to cultural
exchange among different countries and this cultural exchange may lead to harmonization of world cultures with
the result that one day all the people of the world maybe eating the same food, listening to the same music and
speaking the same language.

Topic-002: What is a Global Language?

         A language achieves a global status when it develops a special role recognized in every country. Now the
question arises what determines a special role? If the mother tongue status of a language makes it global then
Spanish should be the global language as it is the mother tongue of over 20 countries around the world. If the
speakers’ number determines it then English is spoken by millions of people around the world.
         However, it is neither the mother tongue status nor the number of speakers which determine the global
status of a language. It is, in fact, identities of the speakers which determine the global status of a language.
Millions of people around the world speak English as a first language. Even a great number of speakers speak it
as their second language. Today, total 1.5 billion speakers of English exist around the world. No other language
can match this degree of growth and development.
         A global language essentially refers to a language that is learned and spoken internationally, and is
characterized not only by the number of its native and second language speakers, but also by its geographical
distribution, and its use in international organizations and in diplomatic relations.
A global language is a language taken up by people in countries in which it is not the mother tongue. It can be
done in two ways:
      By making it the official language of the country (second language)
      By making it a priority in foreign-language teaching e.g. Russian is popular in former Soviet Union
         countries

discusses the role of English as a single global language all over the world and its advantages for the world as
well as the dangers for the minor languages. The course also describes various political, social and historical
contexts which led to the spread of English throughout the world and eventually caused it to become a lingua
franca.

The course aims to:
    understand globalization, global language and the need of a global language
    comprehend the relation between language and identity and the dominance of a global language over
       minor languages.
    have a conceptual understanding of English as native, second, foreign and international language and the
       factors affecting them.
Topic-001: Globalization

         World Englishes is a term coined by BrajKachru (an Indian-American linguist) initially to refer to the
institutionalized varieties of English. Now the term refers to various varieties of English across the world. The
pluralization of World English in the title refers to the large number of varieties that English is accrued as a result
of its contact with sociolinguistic context. It means that English is no longer used by native English speakers in
native English speaking countries like America, Australia, New Zealand, etc. Now English is also used by non-
native English speakers in non-native English speaking countries for various professional, official and
educational purposes. These countries include Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, etc. These distinct
varieties are grouped together under the heading of World Englishes.

         Globalization refers to a great number of things taking place in the world and their interconnectedness. It
is a process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments of different nations. This
interaction can take various forms, e.g. political cooperation among countries with the hope that this kind of co-
operation will help prevent disputes or in case of a dispute will help resolve such disputes. Some examples are
SAARC, European Union and NATO. Another form that this interaction can take is through sharing of ideas and
information. In today’s world sharing of information takes place through social media and internet. This can also
take place with the help of TV programs, films and books.
         Trade and exchange of resources greatly enhances this interaction. Countries like America sell their
finished products and technologies to countries which lack them. Similarly, developing countries sell their
natural resources to the developed countries which need them.
Globalization is not a new phenomenon. For thousands of years countries and later corporation have been selling
and buying things from far off lands. Similarly, for centuries, countries have been investing in enterprises in
foreign countries. It increased as result of technological development. Globalization has also led to cultural
exchange among different countries and this cultural exchange may lead to harmonization of world cultures with
the result that one day all the people of the world maybe eating the same food, listening to the same music and
speaking the same language.

Topic-002: What is a Global Language?

         A language achieves a global status when it develops a special role recognized in every country. Now the
question arises what determines a special role? If the mother tongue status of a language makes it global then
Spanish should be the global language as it is the mother tongue of over 20 countries around the world. If the
speakers’ number determines it then English is spoken by millions of people around the world.
         However, it is neither the mother tongue status nor the number of speakers which determine the global
status of a language. It is, in fact, identities of the speakers which determine the global status of a language.
Millions of people around the world speak English as a first language. Even a great number of speakers speak it
as their second language. Today, total 1.5 billion speakers of English exist around the world. No other language
can match this degree of growth and development.
         A global language essentially refers to a language that is learned and spoken internationally, and is
characterized not only by the number of its native and second language speakers, but also by its geographical
distribution, and its use in international organizations and in diplomatic relations.
A global language is a language taken up by people in countries in which it is not the mother tongue. It can be
done in two ways:
      By making it the official language of the country (second language)

         countries

    • An indigenous language can be adopted as a lingua franca, e.g. Mandarin Chinese
    • A foreign language of a powerful nation becomes lingua franca, e.g. English

What are the main objectives of this course?

How does a language achieve global status?
Answer: A language becomes global when it holds a special role recognized
internationally, not solely based on mother tongue status or speaker numbers.
What determines the global status of a language?
Answer: The global status of a language is determined by the identities of its
speakers, their numbers, geographic distribution, and its use in international
organizations and diplomacy.
What characterizes a global language?
Answer: A global language is spoken and learned internationally, has widespread
use in various countries, and is used for communication beyond native speakers.
How can a language attain the status of being a global language?
Answer: The status of a global language is attained through its recognition as
having a special role that is acknowledged internationally. This recognition goes
beyond the language's native speaker count or its prevalence. Instead, it hinges on

the identity of its speakers, the widespread geographic distribution of its usage, and
its integration into international diplomacy and organizations.
Define a global language and discuss its characteristics.
Answer: A global language is one that is learned and spoken across international
boundaries, serving as a means of communication for speakers beyond just its
native speakers. Its characteristics include:
   •   A diverse range of speakers across various countries.
   •   Its usage not limited to mother tongue status.
   •   Widespread utilization in international organizations and diplomacy.
   •   The capacity to bridge communication gaps among diverse linguistic
       communities.

Why is a common global language necessary?
Answer: A common global language, or lingua franca, is needed to facilitate
effective communication among linguistically diverse communities, overcoming
the limitations of translation.
What is a lingua franca?
Answer: A lingua franca is a language adopted as a common means of
communication between people with different native languages.
What are some needs for a global language in different domains?
Answer: A global language is essential for international forums (e.g., UN),
scientific collaboration, and international business.
Why is the concept of a common global language important?
Answer: The need for a common global language arises from the historical practice
of communication between linguistically diverse communities through translators
and interpreters. Such practices, though essential, were constrained by limitations
in capturing the nuanced emotions and subtleties of communication. A lingua
franca, or common global language, addresses this issue by providing a common

medium for communication, fostering better understanding and more effective
interaction.
Define "lingua franca" and discuss its significance.
Answer: A lingua franca is a language adopted as a means of communication
between individuals whose native languages differ. Its importance lies in its ability
to overcome language barriers, enabling effective communication in various
domains, such as diplomacy, trade, and scholarly collaboration, where clear and
unambiguous understanding is paramount.

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course Learning Theories

        The course gives an engaging overview of the development and concept of World Englishes. The
course discusses the role of English as a single global language all over the world and its advantages for
the world as well as the dangers for the minor languages. The course also describes various political,
social and historical contexts which led to the spread of English throughout the world and eventually
caused it to become a lingua franca.

The course aims to:
   • understand globalization, global language and the need of a global language
   • comprehend the relation between language and identity and the dominance of a global language
       over minor languages.
   • have a conceptual understanding of English as native, second, foreign and international language
       and the factors affecting them.
Topic-001: Globalization

         World Englishes is a term coined by Braj Kachru (an Indian-American linguist) initially to refer
to the institutionalized varieties of English. Now the term refers to various varieties of English across the
world. The pluralization of World English in the title refers to the large number of varieties that English is
accrued as a result of its contact with sociolinguistic context. It means that English is no longer used by
native English speakers in native English speaking countries like America, Australia, New Zealand, etc.
Now English is also used by non-native English speakers in non-native English speaking countries for
various professional, official and educational purposes. These countries include Pakistan, India, Sri
Lanka, Hong Kong, etc. These distinct varieties are grouped together under the heading of World
Englishes.

         Globalization refers to a great number of things taking place in the world and their
interconnectedness. It is a process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and
governments of different nations. This interaction can take various forms, e.g. political cooperation
among countries with the hope that this kind of co-operation will help prevent disputes or in case of a
dispute will help resolve such disputes. Some examples are SAARC, European Union and NATO.
Another form that this interaction can take is through sharing of ideas and information. In today’s world
sharing of information takes place through social media and internet. This can also take place with the
help of TV programs, films and books.
         Trade and exchange of resources greatly enhances this interaction. Countries like America sell
their finished products and technologies to countries which lack them. Similarly, developing countries sell
their natural resources to the developed countries which need them.
Globalization is not a new phenomenon. For thousands of years countries and later corporation have been
selling and buying things from far off lands. Similarly, for centuries, countries have been investing in
enterprises in foreign countries. It increased as result of technological development. Globalization has

also led to cultural exchange among different countries and this cultural exchange may lead to
harmonization of world cultures with the result that one day all the people of the world maybe eating the
same food, listening to the same music and speaking the same language.

Topic-002: What is a Global Language?
         A language achieves a global status when it develops a special role recognized in every country.
Now the question arises what determines a special role? If the mother tongue status of a language makes
it global then Spanish should be the global language as it is the mother tongue of over 20 countries around
the world. If the speakers’ number determines it then English is spoken by millions of people around the
world.
         However, it is neither the mother tongue status nor the number of speakers which determine the
global status of a language. It is, in fact, identities of the speakers which determine the global status of a
language.
Millions of people around the world speak English as a first language. Even a great number of speakers
speak it as their second language. Today, total 1.5 billion speakers of English exist around the world. No
other language can match this degree of growth and development.
         A global language essentially refers to a language that is learned and spoken internationally, and
is characterized not only by the number of its native and second language speakers, but also by its
geographical distribution, and its use in international organizations and in diplomatic relations.
A global language is a language taken up by people in countries in which it is not the mother tongue. It
can be done in two ways:
     • By making it the official language of the country (second language)
     • By making it a priority in foreign-language teaching e.g. Russian is popular in former Soviet
         Union countries

Topic-003: The Need for a Global Language

         There is an urgent need for global language but this need is not new. Linguistically mixed
communities have been communicating with each other for thousands of years. Communication in the
past was through translators and interpreters. Monarchs, kings and ambassadors met with each other in
the presence of interpreters. However, this kind of communication has its own problems. It was restricted
and incomplete information because intensity and mildness of feelings cannot be communicated through
translation. Having a common language (lingua franca) is the solution to this problem. Lingua franca can
be defined in the follow words:

ENG506
➡️ English as a Global Language

English has become the dominant global language, used for international communication in
various contexts. This status has raised concerns about linguistic imperialism, cultural
homogenization, and language shift.

➡️ Dangers of a Global Language

The spread of English as a global language poses dangers, including language endangerment,
cultural loss, and unequal power dynamics. English dominance can marginalize local languages
and cultures.

➡️ Historical, Political and Social Contexts

World Englishes emerged from historical, political, and social contexts, including colonization,
globalization, and technological advancements. These contexts shaped English varieties
worldwide.

➡️ Contact-Induced Varieties of English

Contact-induced varieties result from interactions between English and local languages. Examples
include Singlish (Singaporean English), Nigerian Pidgin English, and Indian English.

➡️ Pidgins and Creoles: Theories of Origin

Pidgins and creoles developed as simplified languages for trade and communication. Theories of
origin include the monogenetic theory (single origin) and polygenetic theory (multiple origins).

➡️ Pidgins and Creoles: Linguistic Features and Characteristics

Pidgins and creoles exhibit simplified grammar, reduced vocabulary, and phonological
adaptations. Examples include Tok Pisin (Papua New Guinea) and Haitian Creole.

➡️ Models and Classifications

Models of World Englishes include Kachru's Three-Circle Model and Schneider's Dynamic
Model. Classifications include inner-circle (native English-speaking countries), outer-circle (post-
colonial countries), and expanding-circle (non-English-speaking countries).

➡️ Kachru’s Three Circle-Model of World English

Kachru's model categorizes English varieties into:

   -   Inner Circle (USA, UK, Australia)
   -   Outer Circle (India, Nigeria, Singapore)
   -   Expanding Circle (China, Japan, Brazil)

➡️ Variations Across Cultures

World Englishes exhibit cultural variations in vocabulary, idioms, and discourse styles. Examples
include African American Vernacular English and Aboriginal Australian English.

➡️ Variations in World Englishes: Linguistic Features

Linguistic variations include phonological (accent), grammatical (verb tense), and lexical
(vocabulary) differences. Examples include Indian English's retroflex consonants and Singaporean
English's particle "lah."

➡️ World Englishes and Intelligibility

Intelligibility concerns arise due to variations in pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar.
However, mutual intelligibility is facilitated through contextual understanding and communication
strategies.

➡️ Standard Language Ideology

The standard language ideology promotes a single, homogeneous English variety. This ideology
overlooks the diversity of World Englishes and perpetuates linguistic inequality.

➡️ Standard English and World Englishes

Standard English coexists with World Englishes, acknowledging diversity while maintaining
communicative efficiency.

➡️ Acculturation

Acculturation refers to the process of cultural adaptation, influencing language use and variation.
World Englishes reflect acculturation through linguistic and cultural borrowings.

Q. Redundancy and repetition with examples
Lexical repetition and redundancy
• An extra element in a sentence or phrase
• Regarded as a universal feature of spoken varieities
Repetition • A repeated occurrence of a linguistic item that may or may not be justified.              „There
were – some very                good houses – rather old               fashioned but good            houses.‟
Repetition
• He sells different different things
 • She cut it into small small pieces
• She drove slowly slowly
 • I don‟t like this type of dress – all frill frill, gather gather
Reduplication The use of double words for one:
•      Flower bouquet • Young kid •                   Cost price •     Proceed to go on
The use of two words for expressing one idea:
•       „….for repairing or laying some sort of underground cables or lines‟
•      „….ever-growing and ever-increasing speeding traffic‟
•      „….without any obstruction and difficulty‟

children and certain pidgins. It Uses high proportion of content, lacks structural words, lacks of

 • Use of a high proportion of content         • Lack of structural words • Lack of morphological change

Q.     What is the role of English after world war-1.explain any two roles? By the 18th
century, three main forces were driving the direction of the English language: (1) to reduce the
language to rule and effect a standard of correct usage; (2) to refine the language by removing
supposed defects and introducing certain improvements; and (3) to fix English permanently in the
desired form. This desire for system and regularity in the language contrasted with the individualism
and spirit of independence characterized by the previous age.
Or Role of English after World War 1 (5) Topic: 28
 Consolidation of English after WWI            • Role as a mediating language     • Spread through colonial
   cultural legacies     • Expansion due to technological revolution.
Q.Contact Literature The literature written in these distinctive varieties of English is often called
contact lit. Writers of contact literature deny that a non-English culture is inexpressible in English and
argue that the cultural material in contact literature will stretch or reshape the expressive qualities of
Eng. The rise of contact literature in English provides an opportunity to study the literary effort of
international writers and to observe the vital process of language change. This change is of special
interest to English teachers and students, since it is their language they are observing, and since the
development it undergoes will make it a more sensitive and authentic vehicle for creative expression
of consciousness in Western and non-Western cultures.
Features of Contact Literature *Foreign influences on English              These varieties undergo a process
of localization • new cultural features           *• types of discourse    • linguistic features Creativity in
contact literature
• Contact literatures exhibit national identity and a linguistic distinctiveness

Q. Write a note on SLA theory constructionA. SLA Theory Construction
• Immigrants or foreign students in universities are used as sources of data
 • Learners of English in the outer and expanding circles are overlooked
 • Little awareness of the factors relevant to English language learning in these contexts
 • Lack of relevance between SLA theories and world Englishes
How do English varieties integrate with SLA Paradigm? (Imp) The goal of SLA is to acquire
native-like competence in the target language, i.e., be as proficient and fluent as a native speaker in
pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary, and also in the sociocultural conventions of language use.
The entire range and depth of input is or ought to be available to the learners so that they can
achieve the goals of language acquisition defined above.
What functions the target language serves in the learners‟ community is irrelevant to SLA.
Learners‟ previous language(s) are not relevant to SLA except as a source of negative transfer, which
is undesirable, or a source of positive transfer, which is acceptable.
Success in SLA depends crucially upon integrative motivation, i.e., the desire to become a part of the
sociocultural milieu of the native speakers of the target language.
Q. Traditional SLA paradigm A. Challenge to traditional SLA paradigm
 • Rejects the attainment of native-like competence as the English learning goal for all learners
• Native speakers not responsible for the standardization of English

ENG506 (MIDS) Fall 2019

Q. Comprehensibility

Involves:

Assigning meaning to utterances

Recognizing an utterance’s referents

Q. Factors which cause variation in language (imp)

    i.         Demographic factor
    ii.        Geographical factor
    iii.       Authoritative factor
    iv.        Codification
    v.         Acceptability factor

Q. Evidence against baby talk? (imp)

Pidgins are far more frequently used among non-Europeans than between Europeans and non-Europeans.

Q. Name of the countries where preferred variety of British English is used.

          North America (USA and Canada),
          Australia,
          New Zealand,
          South Africa

Q. Interoperability

          To understand the purpose and intent of an utterance
          Most complex and most important

Q. Communicative competence

Communicative competence is a term in linguistics which refers to a language user's grammatical knowledge of
syntax, morphology, phonology and the like, as well as social knowledge about how and when to use utterances
appropriately.

Q. Process of the creolization (imp)

Most pidgins are lingua francas, existing to meet temporary local needs

Very few pidgins undergo the process of creolisation.

Q. Functions and use of articles?

A singular countable noun must be preceded by an article

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                                 Page 1

                                    ENG506 (MIDS) Fall 2019
a/an: with a singular countable noun indicates the generic nature of the noun

          A horse runs very fast.
          The: with both singular and plural countable nouns indicate the specific nature of the noun
          The boys are naughty.
          They boys is tall.

With mass nouns to indicate the specific nature of the noun

Q. Misunderstandings about the success of English as an international language.

          Perceived aesthetic qualities
          Clarity of expression
          Literary power
          Religious influence
          Simple structure and grammar

Q. Global vs. standard language

Global language: A language achieves a global status when it develops a special role recognized in every country.

Standard Language: The form of the English language widely accepted as the usual correct form

Q. Lexifer

          Locally coined words and expressions.
          Considered the creativity of New English speakers by many world Englishes scholars.

Q. Name three types of intelligeblities (imp)

    i.         Intelligibility.
    ii.        Comprehensibility.
    iii.       Interpretability.

Q. Define a 'native speaker' in your own words

          The monolingual tenet was central to the colonial agenda
          It marginalizes the English language learners and privileges native speakers
          Extends the colonial agenda of economic exploitation and cultural domination.

Q. What are the advantages and disadvantages of reconceptulization?

• MES is less favorable than BES

• BES removes the distinction between L1 and L2 speakers of English

Determining the difference between bilingual and non-bilingual competence

Q. Write about Conflation of Consonants?

The process of reducing inflected words to their word stem, base or root form. Examples (Caribbean Creoles) /t/ =
/θ/ /d/ = /ð/ /tʃ/ = /ʃ/

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                                  Page 2

                                       ENG506 (MIDS) Fall 2019
Examples (Pacific Pidgin: Tok Pisin Creoles)

/f/ = /p/ friend = pren /s/, / ʃ / = /tʃ/

Q. Note of Kachru Inner Circle?

This classification is in accordance with the three-way categorization of ENL, ESL and EFL. Inner circle includes
the following countries:

                   USA
                   UK
                   Canada
                   Australia
                   New Zealand

English reached these countries as a result of its first diaspora Diaspora The movement or migration of a group of
people away from their established or ancestral homeland English diaspora First diaspora English speakers from
Britain carried the language to Australia, New Zealand, and North America. They established substantial
settlements and displaced the indigenous population Features of the inner circle

                   Traditional monolingual native speakers of English are found
                   English is the first and sometimes the only language
                   Dominant culture is based around English.

Q. Contact literature?

Contact with non-Western cultures and languages enables English to express new linguistic and cultural functions.
Nativized varieties of English are produced through contact of English with new cultures and surrounding
languages. The literature written in distinctive varieties of English is often called contact literature. As English
becomes institutionalized in nations that do not share its Western cultural traditions, the language is broadening.
Beliefs of contact literature writers

                   Some aspects of non-English culture is inexpressible in English.
                   Cultural material in contact literature stretches or reshapes the expressive qualities of English.
                   Provides an exposure to the literary effort of international writers.

Q. Define Creole?

The word comes from the Portuguese word ‘criar’ meaning ‘to nurse’, ‘breed’, ‘bring up’ Pidgins gave rise to
Creole English. A pidgin that has become the first language of a new generation of speakers is called Creole.
Creoles arise when pidgins become mother tongues. Creole. It has native speakers (the children learn the pidgin as
their first language)

Process of creolization

                   Opposed to the process of pidginization
                   Used for a wide range of functions
                   Has a larger vocabulary

Q. Internal factors?

                   Lexicon

2. Bilingual women make choice of a language to severel reasons? Discuss (5)

Bilingual women make language choices to:

   1) Meet the needs of their speech community.
   2) Ensure better future for themselves and their families.
   3) Strengthen the status of English in world communities.

English-speaking bilingual women are considered as innovators of language change

They help in advancing the progress of English and gaining acceptance and importance along
with regional dialects. Women play a key role in the transmission of English in world contexts
and in constructing new identities.

3. Explain the phenomenon of linguistic imperialism in details(5)

Spread of English is equated with linguistic imperialism. It is a sort of imposition of one
language on speakers of other languages. “Linguistic imperialism assumes the active promotion
of the language by the dominant class as an active expression of power of the powerful over the
powerless.” (Phillipson, 1992). “The dominance asserted and maintained by the establishment
and continuous reconstitution of structural and cultural inequalities between English and other
languages.” (Phillipson, 2006). Dominance of English is considered as letting or facilitating
cultural, economic, and sociopolitical hegemony of Anglo- and Eurocentric views over the rest
of the world

Paradox of linguistic imperialism:

• Linguistic imperialism as an outdated concept

• English as a tool empowerment and emancipation

• Widespread demand for more access to English

• Example: African American English (AAE),

• Perceived as homogeneous

• A strong degree of mixing, mutual accommodation, and koinéization

• Dialect studies show a great deal of phonetic, lexical, and grammatical variability

• No nationally uniform standard accent of American English

• Diversity has replaced homogeneity

Globalisation: Definition: The process of increasing global connectivity and
interdependence.
 What is a Global Language?: A language that is widely used and accepted for
international communication.
 The Need for a Global Language in Present Times: Globalization has created a need
for a common language to facilitate international communication and commerce.
 What Makes a Global Language?
         Widespread use and acceptance
         Simple and adaptable grammar and vocabulary
         Economic and cultural influence of its native speakers
 Emergence of English as a Global Language: English has become the dominant global
language due to British colonialism, economic influence, and cultural spread.
 Change in the Status of English: From a language of colonialism to a language of
international communication and commerce.
 Dangers of Global Language
     Undue Empowerment of Users: Dominant language speakers may impose their
        language and culture on others.
     Linguistic Complacency: Native speakers may become complacent and neglect
        language maintenance.
     Loss of Linguistic Diversity: Global languages may lead to the decline of local
        languages and cultures.
 The Issues of National and Cultural Identity: Global languages can threaten local
identities and cultures.
 Introducing World Englishes: World Englishes refers to the diverse varieties of English
spoken globally, each with unique features and contexts
 Origins: World Englishes emerged from the spread of English through colonialism, trade,
and cultural exchange
 Spread of English Through Migrations and Settlement: America: English was brought
to America by British colonizers and settlers. American English developed distinct
features, such as vocabulary and pronunciation differences.
 Spread of English through Migrations and Settlements: New Zealand: English was
introduced by British colonizers and missionaries. New Zealand English has unique
features, such as Maori loanwords and a distinct accent.

 Spread of English: Caribbean: English was brought by British colonizers, African
slaves, and indentured servants. Caribbean Englishes (e.g., Jamaican, Trinidadian) have
creole features and African influences.
 Spread of English: South East Asia: English was introduced by British and American
colonizers, traders, and missionaries. South East Asian Englishes (e.g., Singaporean,
Malaysian) have distinct features, such as loanwords and accents.
 Spread of English: South Africa: English was brought by British colonizers and settlers.
South African English has unique features, such as Afrikaans loanwords and a distinct
accent.
 Spread of English: Africa: English was introduced by British colonizers, missionaries,
and traders. African Englishes (e.g., Nigerian, Ghanaian) have distinct features, such as
loanwords and accents.
Spread of English: South Asia: English was introduced by British colonizers and traders.
South Asian Englishes (e.g., Indian, Pakistani) have distinct features, such as loanwords
and accents.
 Political Developments:
         Colonialism and imperialism led to the spread of English globally.
         English became a language of power, education, and international
            communication.
         Post-colonialism and globalization have further spread English, with varying
            impacts on local languages and cultures.
 Technological and Industrial Developments: The spread of English worldwide is linked
to technological advancements, industrialization, and globalization, which have increased
international communication, trade, and cultural exchange.
 Social and Cultural Trends: English has become a symbol of modernity, globalization,
and cultural exchange, influencing social and cultural norms worldwide.
 International Travel: With increased travel and tourism, English has become the primary
language for communication among people from different countries.
 English as a Lingua Franca: English serves as a common language for international
communication, enabling people who speak different native languages to communicate.
 Pidgins and Creoles: These are simplified languages that emerge as a result of contact
between groups with no common language. Pidgins are used for basic communication,
while Creoles are more complex and become native languages.
 Process of Pidginization: This is the development of a pidgin language, often for trade
or communication between groups.
 Process of Creolization: This is the development of a creole language, often from a
pidgin, as it becomes a native language for a community.
 Geographical Distribution: English is spoken worldwide, with varying forms and
accents depending on the region.

 Independent Parallel Development Theory: This theory suggests that similar linguistic
features in different varieties of English are due to independent development rather than
direct influence.
 Nautical Jargon Theory: This theory proposes that nautical terminology and sailor slang
influenced the development of pidgins and Creoles.
 Monogenesis Theory: This theory suggests that all pidgins and Creoles come from a
single, ancestral language.
Afrogenesis Hypothesis: A subset of Monogenesis Theory, proposing that all pidgins and
Creoles originated from African languages.
 Baby Talk Theory: This theory suggests that pidgins and Creoles developed from
simplified language used with children or foreigners.
 Theory of Relexification
         This theory proposes that creole languages are formed through a process of
            relexification, where the vocabulary of an existing language (the lexifier) is
            replaced with that of another language (the substrate).
         This process occurs when two groups with different languages interact, and the
            substrate language influences the grammar and vocabulary of the lexifier
            language.
         Relexification theory suggests that creoles retain the grammatical structure of
            the substrate language, but adopt the vocabulary of the lexifier language.

         (ENG506) World Englishes

Lesson-01

                 English as a Global Language

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course Learning Theories
What is the main focus of this course?
Answer: The course provides an overview of World Englishes, discussing its
development and concept as a global language, along with its advantages and
potential risks.
What are the goals of this course?
Answer: The goals of this course include understanding globalization and the need
for a global language, exploring the relationship between language and identity,
and gaining insights into different types of English.
 What are the different contexts that contributed to English becoming a lingua
franca?
Answer: Various political, social, and historical contexts, as well as technological
advancements, led to English becoming a widely spoken global language.
What is the primary focus and content of this course?
Answer: This course offers a comprehensive overview of World Englishes, delving
into their development and conceptualization as a global linguistic phenomenon. It

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             1

explores both the advantages of English's global dominance and the potential risks
it poses to minor languages. Furthermore, the course examines the historical,
political, and social contexts that have propelled English to its status as a
worldwide lingua franca.
What are the main objectives of this course?
Answer: The primary objectives of this course are threefold:
   • To foster a deep understanding of concepts like globalization and the
     necessity of a global language.
   • To elucidate the intricate connection between language and identity,
     particularly in light of the overpowering influence of a global language on
     lesser-known languages.
   • To provide students with a holistic grasp of English's various roles, ranging
     from native and second language usage to its status as an international and
     foreign language, while also considering the factors impacting each role.
Topic-002: What is a Global Language?

How does a language achieve global status?
Answer: A language becomes global when it holds a special role recognized
internationally, not solely based on mother tongue status or speaker numbers.
What determines the global status of a language?
Answer: The global status of a language is determined by the identities of its
speakers, their numbers, geographic distribution, and its use in international
organizations and diplomacy.
What characterizes a global language?
Answer: A global language is spoken and learned internationally, has widespread
use in various countries, and is used for communication beyond native speakers.
How can a language attain the status of being a global language?
Answer: The status of a global language is attained through its recognition as
having a special role that is acknowledged internationally. This recognition goes
beyond the language's native speaker count or its prevalence. Instead, it hinges on

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            2

the identity of its speakers, the widespread geographic distribution of its usage, and
its integration into international diplomacy and organizations.
Define a global language and discuss its characteristics.
Answer: A global language is one that is learned and spoken across international
boundaries, serving as a means of communication for speakers beyond just its
native speakers. Its characteristics include:
   •   A diverse range of speakers across various countries.
   •   Its usage not limited to mother tongue status.
   •   Widespread utilization in international organizations and diplomacy.
   •   The capacity to bridge communication gaps among diverse linguistic
       communities.
Topic-003: The Need for a Global Language

Why is a common global language necessary?
Answer: A common global language, or lingua franca, is needed to facilitate
effective communication among linguistically diverse communities, overcoming
the limitations of translation.
What is a lingua franca?
Answer: A lingua franca is a language adopted as a common means of
communication between people with different native languages.
What are some needs for a global language in different domains?
Answer: A global language is essential for international forums (e.g., UN),
scientific collaboration, and international business.
Why is the concept of a common global language important?
Answer: The need for a common global language arises from the historical practice
of communication between linguistically diverse communities through translators
and interpreters. Such practices, though essential, were constrained by limitations
in capturing the nuanced emotions and subtleties of communication. A lingua
franca, or common global language, addresses this issue by providing a common

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              3

medium for communication, fostering better understanding and more effective
interaction.
Define "lingua franca" and discuss its significance.
Answer: A lingua franca is a language adopted as a means of communication
between individuals whose native languages differ. Its importance lies in its ability
to overcome language barriers, enabling effective communication in various
domains, such as diplomacy, trade, and scholarly collaboration, where clear and
unambiguous understanding is paramount.
Topic-004: What Makes a Global Language?
What are some common misconceptions about the factors that contribute to a
language's success?
Answer: There are misunderstandings about aesthetic qualities, clarity, literary
power, religious influence, and structural features as determinants of a language's
success.
Why doesn't a language become global solely based on structural properties
or vocabulary?
Answer: A language's global status is not determined by its structural properties,

Lesson-06

          Contact Induced Varieties of English
Topic 031: Pidgins and Creoles
What is a pidgin?
A pidgin is a simplified language that emerges when people with no common
language need to communicate.
Define "language contact."
Language contact is when speakers of different languages interact, resulting in
the transfer of linguistic features.
How does the term "pidgin" originate?
It originates from various sources, including a Chinese corruption of "business"
and the Portuguese word "ocupaçao."

What is a creole?
A creole is a pidgin that becomes the first language of a new generation of
speakers.
Explain the concept of "language contact" and its relevance to pidgins.
"Language contact" is a phenomenon where speakers of different languages
interact, leading to the transfer of linguistic features between them. In the
context of pidgins, language contact is essential because it is the interaction
between speakers of different languages that necessitates the creation of a
simplified communication system, or a pidgin. (Topic 031)
Topic 032: Process of Pidginization-I
What historical events contributed to pidginization?
European colonization in Africa and Asia, as well as New World slavery,
contributed to pidginization.
Why were slaves drawn from various language backgrounds?
Slaves were deliberately drawn from different language backgrounds to prevent
rebellion against their masters.
What is the process of pidginization?
Pidginization is the simplification of a language used by speakers separated by
different languages.
Explain the process of pidginization in terms of language simplification.
Pidginization involves the simplification of a language used by groups of speakers
who are separated from each other by different languages. This simplification
occurs because speakers of different languages must find a common way to
communicate, leading to the creation of a simplified linguistic system or pidgin.
(Topic 032)
Topic 033: Process of Pidginization-II
What characterizes the simplification of a dominant language in pidginization?

It involves simplifying grammar, using fewer words, and having a restricted range
of phonological and syntactic options.
Provide examples of words in a pidgin.
Examples include "bros" for friend, "show" for come or arrive, and "haus" for
house.
What are common views about pidgins?
Common views include considering pidgins as marginal, degenerate, or
imperfectly learned languages.
Can you provide examples of words from a pidgin language?
Certainly, in a pidgin language, words are often simplified and may include terms
like "bros" for friend, "show" for to come or arrive, and "haus" for house. These
examples illustrate the simplification of words in pidgin languages for easier
communication. (Topic 033)
Topic 034: Process of Creolization-I
How does a creole differ from a pidgin?
A creole evolves from a pidgin into a richer language and has native speakers.
What is the origin of the term "creole"?
It comes from the Portuguese word "criar," meaning to nurse, breed, or bring up.
What are the differences between pidgins and creoles in terms of vocabulary
and grammar?
Creoles have a larger vocabulary and more complicated grammatical resources
compared to pidgins.
Topic 035: Process of Creolization-II
Q: What is a creole continuum, and how does it arise?
A creole continuum arises from the relationship with a superstrate language, like
Standard English.
What is "decreolization"?

Decreolization is the process where an increase in varieties leads to more
influence from the Standard English, often involving social stratification.
What are the components of the creole continuum?
It includes the acrolect (high speech), mesolect (middle speech), and basilect (low
speech).
Topic 036: Geographical Distribution
Where are pidgins and creoles primarily distributed?
They are mainly found in the equatorial belt, including the Caribbean, the coasts
of South America, West Africa, and islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
How many English-based pidgins and creoles are listed by Hancock?
Hancock lists 35 English-based pidgins and creoles out of a total of 127.
How does language distribution reflect the history of regions?
The language distribution reflects the social and political history of regions, with
some countries having only English-based creoles, and others having only French-
based ones.

Lesson-07

         Pidgins and Creoles: Theories of Origin
Topic 037: Independent Parallel Development Theory
What are the three main groups of Theories of Origin for pidgins and creoles?
Polygenesis (Evolved from various sources) 2. Monogenesis (Evolved from a single
source) 3. Universal strategies (Derived from universal strategies)
What does the Independent Parallel Development Theory (Polygenetic) suggest
about the development of pidgins and creoles?
Pidgins and creoles developed independently from a variety of origins, with
similarities due to shared circumstances of origin.

Topic 038: Nautical Jargon Theory
How did the Nautical Jargon Theory explain the development of pidgins?
It suggested that pidgins developed from a shipboard lingua franca influenced by
nautical jargon, passed on to different cultures through sailors on trading routes.
What are some characteristics of the Nautical Jargon Theory?
It consisted of a core vocabulary of nautical items and a simplified grammar.

"hoist."

the transfer of linguistic features.

It originates from various sources, including a Chinese corruption of "business"
and the Portuguese word "ocupaçao."

What is a creole?
A creole is a pidgin that becomes the first language of a new generation of
speakers.
Explain the concept of "language contact" and its relevance to pidgins.
"Language contact" is a phenomenon where speakers of different languages
interact, leading to the transfer of linguistic features between them. In the
context of pidgins, language contact is essential because it is the interaction
between speakers of different languages that necessitates the creation of a
simplified communication system, or a pidgin. (Topic 031)
Topic 032: Process of Pidginization-I
What historical events contributed to pidginization?
European colonization in Africa and Asia, as well as New World slavery,
contributed to pidginization.
Why were slaves drawn from various language backgrounds?
Slaves were deliberately drawn from different language backgrounds to prevent
rebellion against their masters.
What is the process of pidginization?
Pidginization is the simplification of a language used by speakers separated by
different languages.
Explain the process of pidginization in terms of language simplification.
Pidginization involves the simplification of a language used by groups of speakers
who are separated from each other by different languages. This simplification
occurs because speakers of different languages must find a common way to
communicate, leading to the creation of a simplified linguistic system or pidgin.

What characterizes the simplification of a dominant language in pidginization?

It involves simplifying grammar, using fewer words, and having a restricted range
of phonological and syntactic options.

Examples include "bros" for friend, "show" for come or arrive, and "haus" for
house.
What are common views about pidgins?
Common views include considering pidgins as marginal, degenerate, or
imperfectly learned languages.
Can you provide examples of words from a pidgin language?
Certainly, in a pidgin language, words are often simplified and may include terms
like "bros" for friend, "show" for to come or arrive, and "haus" for house. These
examples illustrate the simplification of words in pidgin languages for easier
communication. (Topic 033)

How does a creole differ from a pidgin?
A creole evolves from a pidgin into a richer language and has native speakers.
What is the origin of the term "creole"?
It comes from the Portuguese word "criar," meaning to nurse, breed, or bring up.
What are the differences between pidgins and creoles in terms of vocabulary
and grammar?
Creoles have a larger vocabulary and more complicated grammatical resources
compared to pidgins.

A creole continuum arises from the relationship with a superstrate language, like
Standard English.

Decreolization is the process where an increase in varieties leads to more

What are the components of the creole continuum?
It includes the acrolect (high speech), mesolect (middle speech), and basilect (low
speech).

They are mainly found in the equatorial belt, including the Caribbean, the coasts

The language distribution reflects the social and political history of regions, with

World Englishes
  (ENG506)

                                                                                             Lesson-01

                                 English as a Global Language

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course Learning Theories

The course gives an engaging overview of the development and concept of World Englishes. The course
discusses the role of English as a single global language all over the world and its advantages for the world
as well as the dangers for the minor languages. The course also describes various political, social and
historical contexts which led to the spread of English throughout the world and eventually caused it to
become a lingua franca.

The course aims to:
   • understand globalization, global language and the need of a global language
   • comprehend the relation between language and identity and the dominance of a global language
       over minor languages.
   • have a conceptual understanding of English as native, second, foreign and international language
       and the factors affecting them.
Topic-001: Globalization

         World Englishes is a term coined by Braj Kachru (an Indian-American linguist) initially to refer to
the institutionalized varieties of English. Now the term refers to various varieties of English across the
world. The pluralization of World English in the title refers to the large number of varieties that English is
accrued as a result of its contact with sociolinguistic context. It means that English is no longer used by
native English speakers in native English speaking countries like America, Australia, New Zealand, etc.
Now English is also used by non-native English speakers in non-native English speaking countries for
various professional, official and educational purposes. These countries include Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka,
Hong Kong, etc. These distinct varieties are grouped together under the heading of World Englishes.

         Globalization refers to a great number of things taking place in the world and their
interconnectedness. It is a process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and
governments of different nations. This interaction can take various forms, e.g. political cooperation among
countries with the hope that this kind of co-operation will help prevent disputes or in case of a dispute will
help resolve such disputes. Some examples are SAARC, European Union and NATO. Another form that
this interaction can take is through sharing of ideas and information. In today’s world sharing of information
takes place through social media and internet. This can also take place with the help of TV programs, films
and books.
         Trade and exchange of resources greatly enhances this interaction. Countries like America sell their
finished products and technologies to countries which lack them. Similarly, developing countries sell their
natural resources to the developed countries which need them.
Globalization is not a new phenomenon. For thousands of years countries and later corporation have been
selling and buying things from far off lands. Similarly, for centuries, countries have been investing in
enterprises in foreign countries. It increased as result of technological development. Globalization has also
led to cultural exchange among different countries and this cultural exchange may lead to harmonization of

world cultures with the result that one day all the people of the world maybe eating the same food, listening
to the same music and speaking the same language.

Topic-002: What is a Global Language?
        A language achieves a global status when it develops a special role recognized in every country.
Now the question arises what determines a special role? If the mother tongue status of a language makes it
global then Spanish should be the global language as it is the mother tongue of over 20 countries around
the world. If the speakers’ number determines it then English is spoken by millions of people around the
world.
        However, it is neither the mother tongue status nor the number of speakers which determine the
global status of a language. It is, in fact, identities of the speakers which determine the global status of a
language.
Millions of people around the world speak English as a first language. Even a great number of speakers
speak it as their second language. Today, total 1.5 billion speakers of English exist around the world. No
other language can match this degree of growth and development.
        A global language essentially refers to a language that is learned and spoken internationally, and is
characterized not only by the number of its native and second language speakers, but also by its
geographical distribution, and its use in international organizations and in diplomatic relations.
A global language is a language taken up by people in countries in which it is not the mother tongue. It can
be done in two ways:
    • By making it the official language of the country (second language)
    • By making it a priority in foreign-language teaching e.g. Russian is popular in former Soviet Union
        countries

Topic-003: The Need for a Global Language

         There is an urgent need for global language but this need is not new. Linguistically mixed
communities have been communicating with each other for thousands of years. Communication in the past
was through translators and interpreters. Monarchs, kings and ambassadors met with each other in the
presence of interpreters. However, this kind of communication has its own problems. It was restricted and
incomplete information because intensity and mildness of feelings cannot be communicated through
translation. Having a common language (lingua franca) is the solution to this problem. Lingua franca can
be defined in the follow words:
         A lingua franca is a language that is adopted as a common language between speakers whose native
languages are different.

Choice of a language as the lingua franca
   • A simplified language used by different trading communities (Pidgin)
